opis: The Bible refuses a simple math of guilt and punishment. What does it give the one who suffers instead of a formula?
zdanie: The Bible doesn’t tell me why I suffer. It tells me it isn’t a sentence passed on me, and it tells me who is with me.

elementy.tekst: This meeting doesn’t answer the question “why.” It shows which answers the Bible refuses. It refuses the math in which every misfortune is payment for a specific sin. It refuses it in the Book of Job, and it refuses it through the mouth of Jesus, twice. In place of that it offers no formula. It offers a God who comes, a Jesus who acts, and a Spirit who groans along with us.
**Where the landmines are:**

pozycje: There is almost certainly someone at the table who is suffering right now, or watching someone they love suffer. For them this isn’t a topic; it’s their life.

The group will want to comfort with ready-made lines: “God has a plan,” “everything happens for a reason,” “God never gives you more than you can handle.” That is exactly what Job’s friends did, and God said they had not spoken accurately about Him.
Someone may hear Luke 13 as a threat. There Jesus is speaking to people who are commenting on someone else’s misfortune, not to those it happened to.
Someone may carry a conviction that their illness or loss is a punishment. Don’t drag that out in front of the group.

elementy.tekst: **What not to do:** don’t explain anyone’s suffering to them. Don’t end the meeting with a sentence that explains everything. If a question is left unanswered at the end, the meeting has succeeded.
Think of something someone said to you during a hard time that helped, or something that hurt. Share only the sentence, without the story behind it.
answer first, and keep it short. Don’t comment on anyone else’s answer. If someone doesn’t want to speak, move on without pausing.

akapity: One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came with them. “Where have you come from?” said the LORD to Satan. “From roaming through the earth,” he replied, “and walking back and forth in it.” Then the LORD said to Satan, “Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil.” Satan answered the LORD, “Does Job fear God for nothing? Have You not placed a hedge on every side around him and his household and all that he owns? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land. But stretch out Your hand and strike all that he has, and he will surely curse You to Your face.” “Very well,” said the LORD to Satan. “Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself.” Then Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.

elementy.tekst: In a single day Job loses his flocks, his servants, and his ten children.

akapity: Then Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped, saying: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD.” In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing.

elementy.tekst: The reader knows something Job won’t find out even by the end of the book. **What exactly do we know that he doesn’t? How does that change the way we hear his words, “the LORD has taken away”?**
Satan doesn’t accuse Job of any sin. **So what does he accuse him of? And who else is touched by that accusation?**
**According to this text, what is the reason for Job’s misfortune: his guilt, or something else entirely?**

Satan’s question is this: does anyone love God for nothing, or only for what they get from Him? It is a charge against Job and at the same time against God, that He buys love with protection. So Job suffers not in spite of his faithfulness but because of it. From the very first page, the book rules out the answer his friends will defend.

akapity: While he was still speaking, another messenger came and reported: “The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants, and I alone have escaped to tell you!”

Then the LORD said to Satan, “Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil. He still retains his integrity, even though you incited Me against him to ruin him without cause.”

elementy.tekst: The servant who survived calls what fell from heaven “the fire of God.” **Would a reader who knows the conversation in verses 6-12 call it the same thing? What does that say about statements like “God did this to me”?**
God Himself says that Job is suffering “without cause.” **What does that phrase do to every attempt to find the cause in Job?**

“For nothing” in Satan’s question in Job 1:9 and “without cause” in God’s words in Job 2:3 are the same word in Hebrew, `chinnam`. Satan asks whether Job loves `chinnam`, that is, without being paid. God answers that Job suffers `chinnam`, that is, for no reason. The book fastens both ends together with one word: a love that is not payment, and a suffering that is not punishment.

akapity: Now when Job’s three friends—Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite—heard about all this adversity that had come upon him, each of them came from his home, and they met together to go and sympathize with Job and comfort him. When they lifted up their eyes from afar, they could barely recognize Job. They began to weep aloud, and each man tore his robe and threw dust in the air over his head. Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was.

elementy.tekst: Then they start talking. Eliphaz speaks first.

akapity: Consider now, I plead: Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed? As I have observed, those who plow iniquity and those who sow trouble reap the same.

elementy.tekst: The conversation goes on for more than thirty chapters. At the end, God gives His verdict on it.

akapity: After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has.

elementy.tekst: **What did the friends do right during the first seven days? At what point did things start to go wrong?**
Eliphaz’s words sound godly and logical. **What exactly is he claiming about the world? What follows from that for the man sitting in front of him in the ashes?**
The friends defended God, and Job argued with Him. **Why does God say that it was Job who spoke accurately about Him?**

The friends don’t question a single truth of the faith. They believe that God is just and that evil has consequences. Their mistake lies in how they apply it: they turn a general principle into a verdict on a specific person. They came to give hope, and they gave guilt instead. God responds to this with an anger found nowhere else in the book. In defending Him, they turned Him into someone who kills children for a father’s hidden sin.

akapity: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: “Who is this who obscures My counsel by words without knowledge? Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding. Who fixed its measurements? Surely you know! Or who stretched a measuring line across it? On what were its foundations set, or who laid its cornerstone, while the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?

elementy.tekst: God speaks for four chapters. Not once does He mention the conversation with Satan. Job answers briefly.

akapity: My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.

elementy.tekst: Throughout the book Job demanded an explanation. **What did he get instead? Why was that enough for him?**
**What is the difference between “My ears had heard of You” and what Job says about himself now? Which of the two helps more in suffering?**

bloki.tytul: A Confession in the Middle of the Darkness

akapity: But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth. Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God. I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger. How my heart yearns within me!

elementy.tekst: These words come in the middle of the book, between one complaint and the next, before God has said anything. **How does Job know this, when nothing in his situation points to it?**
In the same book, Job says very sharp things to God and confesses that his Redeemer lives. **Does one rule out the other? What does God think about that, judging by Job 42:7?**

akapity: Now as Jesus was passing by, He saw a man blind from birth, and His disciples asked Him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him. While it is daytime, we must do the works of Him who sent Me. Night is coming, when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” When Jesus had said this, He spit on the ground, made some mud, and applied it to the man’s eyes. Then He told him, “Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So the man went and washed, and came back seeing.

elementy.tekst: The disciples give Jesus two options to choose from. **What does Jesus do with their question? What question does He answer instead?**
The disciples look at the blind man and see a theological puzzle. **What does Jesus see? How can we tell from the text?**
**How does a person feel when people around them wonder out loud whose fault it is? Do we ever do that?**

In the ancient world, guilt was often recognized by misfortune. A person didn’t conclude they had done wrong because their conscience troubled them. They concluded it because they fell ill, lost someone close, or suffered disaster. Misfortune was a sign, and the sign sent you looking for sin. So the disciples’ question isn’t malicious. It’s ordinary; everyone thought that way. That makes Jesus’ answer all the stronger, since He chooses neither of the two options offered.

akapity: So a second time they called for the man who had been blind and said, “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.” He answered, “Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!”

elementy.tekst: The interrogators say, “We know.” The healed man says, “I do not know,” and “There is one thing I do know.” **In this chapter, who is sure of their theology, and who can see? What does that mean for our conversations about suffering?**

bloki.tytul: Tension: “So That the Works of God Would Be Displayed”

elementy.tekst: Jesus’ words in verse 3 can hurt. Did God make a man blind for years just to have an opportunity for a miracle?

The oldest Greek manuscripts have no punctuation. Periods and commas are added by editors and translators, and English versions often also supply words like “this happened,” which are not in the Greek. The same words can be divided differently: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned. But so that the works of God would be displayed in him, we must do the works of Him who sent Me while it is daytime.” Read that way, Jesus doesn’t give a reason for the blindness at all. He says what needs to be done now.
**How does the picture of God change depending on where we put the period?** Which reading fits better with what Jesus does in the following verses?

Even with the traditional punctuation, Jesus doesn’t say where the blindness came from, only where this story is heading. **What is the difference between asking “why” and asking “toward what”? Which one does Jesus treat as worth answering?**

akapity: At that time some of those present told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. To this He replied, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this fate? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish. Or those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam collapsed on them: Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.”

elementy.tekst: Jesus adds a second example Himself. The first is a crime committed by those in power; the second is a building collapse. **What does His answer have in common in both cases? What conclusion about the victims does He forbid?**

Jesus turns the conversation away from the victims and toward those who are talking about them. **Why does He do that? Whom is the call to repent addressed to, and whom is it certainly not addressed to?**

In the Bible, to repent means to turn around: a change of mind and of direction. Jesus isn’t threatening the victims. He is speaking to people who comment on someone else’s tragedy from a safe distance and try to work out what the victims did to deserve it. He takes that distance away from them. Misfortune is not a ranking of sinners.

akapity: One Sabbath Jesus was teaching in one of the synagogues, and a woman there had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years. She was hunched over and could not stand up straight. When Jesus saw her, He called her over and said, “Woman, you are set free from your disability.” Then He placed His hands on her, and immediately she straightened up and began to glorify God. But the synagogue leader was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. “There are six days for work,” he told the crowd. “So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath.” “You hypocrites!” the Lord replied. “Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water? Then should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years, be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?” When Jesus said this, all His adversaries were humiliated. And the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing.

elementy.tekst: This is the same chapter, a few verses later. **To whom does Jesus attribute this woman’s illness? What does He call her?**

The same image comes up three times in this scene: the woman set free, the ox untied, the daughter of Abraham released from her bondage. **If illness is a bond and not a punishment, whose side is God on?**

akapity: I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us. The creation waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God. We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time. Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.

In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God. And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.

elementy.tekst: In this passage, three parties groan. **Who are they? What does that say about where God stands in relation to suffering: above it, beside it, or within it?**
Read verse 28 word by word. **Does Paul write that everything that happens to us is good? What exactly does he write?**
Paul speaks of a world “subjected to futility” and in “bondage to decay.” **How does that description of the world change the question, “Why did this happen to me?”**

akapity: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God. For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows.

For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin. Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.

elementy.tekst: Paul doesn’t write that God explains our troubles. He writes that God comforts us in them. **According to these two passages, what does the comfort God gives look like? How is it different from the comfort Job’s friends gave?**
**Who was able to be with you in a hard time because they had been through something themselves?** What did they do differently from everyone else?

bloki.tytul: Tension: “All Things Together for the Good”

elementy.tekst: Romans 8:28 is sometimes quoted as the sentence that ends the conversation. But Paul doesn’t say that evil is good in disguise, or that God sends it for our benefit. He says that God works in all things, including the things He did not want.

akapity: As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.

elementy.tekst: Joseph doesn’t tell his brothers that selling him was good. He calls it evil. **So what does he attribute to God? How does that help us read Romans 8:28?**
Joseph said this decades later, and he said it about himself. **What happens when someone else says the same sentence to a person who is still sitting in the pit?**
**Which ready-made explanations of suffering have you been carrying around for a long time?** Where did you get them: from home, from church, from your own guesses?
Think of someone who is suffering right now. **What in today’s texts shows you how to be with them? What should you definitely not say to them?**
If you’d like to share: **is there a “why” in your life that never got an answer?** You don’t have to say what it’s about. It’s enough to say what you do with it today.

bloki.tytul: A Question Without an Easy Answer

elementy.tekst: From the first page, the reader of Job knows what is at stake. Job never finds out, not even when God finally speaks. **Why didn’t God tell him? Would Job’s faith have been the same faith if he had known what was going on behind the scenes?**

The conversation in Job 1 raises a question the text doesn’t settle: why does God agree at all? One answer notes that if God had refused, He would have confirmed the charge that He shields His people to buy their loyalty. **Is that answer enough for you? What in it helps, and what still chafes?**

akapity: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword? As it is written: “For Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.” No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

elementy.tekst: Paul doesn’t promise that trouble, famine, and sword will pass us by. He lists them as things that will come. **So what does he promise? Is that little or a lot?**
don’t close these questions. The text leaves them open, and the group can too.
The Bible doesn’t tell me why I suffer. It tells me it isn’t a sentence passed on me, and it tells me who is with me.
**Verse to remember:** Romans 8:26 or Job 42:5.

This week, when you hear about someone’s misfortune, catch the first thought that comes to mind. Check whether there’s a quiet “they probably brought it on themselves” in it. Don’t judge yourself for it. Just notice how deeply the math of Job’s friends is rooted in us.

If you carry a conviction that some loss or illness of yours is a punishment, tell God so directly, in your own words. Then read again what Jesus said to the disciples beside the blind man, and stay with that sentence.
**For the brave:** go to someone who is suffering and don’t say anything wise. Just sit with them. For seven days, Job’s friends did exactly what was needed.

**Someone at the table is in fresh suffering: a diagnosis, the death of someone close, a family falling apart.** The meeting is then above all for them, but not about them. Don’t ask them anything directly, and don’t use them as an illustration. If they start talking, the group listens. Nobody gives advice, nobody explains, nobody tells their own story in response. After the meeting, stay with the person or set up a time to talk. The group walks alongside; it doesn’t heal. If you hear about suicidal thoughts or abuse, don’t carry it alone. Make sure they know about a crisis line in your country and your local emergency number.

**Pious clichés: “God has a plan,” “everything happens for a reason,” “God never gives you more than you can handle,” “it must have been meant to be.”** Interrupt gently, and right away. You can say, “Let’s stop for a moment. Job’s friends also said things that sounded good. Let’s check whether that sentence is in the text in front of us.” Usually it isn’t. Don’t shame the person who said it. Most often they say it because they are afraid themselves.

**“It’s because of sin,” or “God is punishing me.”** Go back to the text: God says of Job “without cause,” and Jesus says, “Neither this man nor his parents.” Don’t deny that sin can have consequences, because it can. Show the difference between a consequence and a sentence. If someone says this about themselves, talk with them after the meeting.

**“So how could God make a bet with Satan over a human being?”** That’s an honest question, and the text provokes it. Don’t defend God faster than the book does. You can say that Job asked sharper questions, and it was Job of whom God said that he had spoken accurately. If you have time, turn to the questions in level 3.

**Someone tells about a healing or a miraculous rescue, and next to them sits someone for whom things didn’t work out.** Say thank you, and don’t build a conclusion on it. Point out that in the same New Testament some people are healed and others are not, and no one is given an explanation for the difference.
**The group falls silent after a question.** With this topic, silence is appropriate. Don’t fill it. Count to ten in your head, and only then repeat the question in the same words.

**The conversation picks up so much that you won’t get through the material.** Skip block 3 and block 5. Blocks 1, 2, 4, and 6 carry the whole: Job is not guilty, the friends are wrong, Jesus rejects the math, the Spirit groans along with us.
